brief: Write a newsletter for engineers about making AI tool retries safe and reversible. Explain how to distinguish read-only retries from actions that can duplicate side effects. Use a clearly hypothetical support-workflow example, an idempotency key, checking the outcome before retrying, a bounded retry limit and backoff, and human handoff when state is uncertain. Include an actionable checklist and limitations: compensation is not always an undo, and irreversible actions require confirmation. Do not claim measured results or cite unsupplied facts. Use a concise email subject, 400–700 words, and at least three descriptive plain-text section headings.

title: Stop AI retries from double-charging your users
content:
A single AI-driven retry can silently double-charge a customer while your logs still look “successful.”

Principle: separate reads from actions

Start with one concrete rule: treat every AI tool call as either read-only or side-effectful, and design retries differently for each.

Read-only calls are safe to retry. Examples: fetch ticket details, generate a summary, check current balance. You can retry on timeouts with backoff and almost no risk.

Side-effectful calls are different. Examples: issue a refund, send an email, cancel a subscription. Here, a naive retry can duplicate the action.

So you make side-effectful retries explicit transactions:

- Attach an idempotency key to each unique intent.
- Store and inspect the outcome for that key before retrying.
- Apply bounded retries with backoff.
- Hand off to a human when state is unclear.

Hypothetical support workflow: AI-driven refunds

Imagine a support system where an AI agent helps with refunds.

1) The agent decides a user should get a $20 refund for ticket T123.
2) It calls a Refund API through your orchestration layer.

You generate an idempotency key like: "refund:T123:20:USD". The Refund API stores:
- key
- status (pending, succeeded, failed, unknown)
- external references (payment provider id)

First attempt:
- The call goes out.
- You get a network timeout.
- The AI tool framework wants to retry.

Before retrying, your orchestration layer:
- Looks up the idempotency key.
- Sees status=pending, no final outcome.

You apply a small bounded retry policy: for example, 3 attempts with exponential backoff. On the second attempt, the provider replies "refund succeeded". You mark the key as succeeded and store the provider reference.

Later, the AI agent or a human clicks "retry refund" again for the same ticket and amount. The system:
- Recomputes the same idempotency key.
- Finds status=succeeded.
- Returns the recorded success to the caller instead of talking to the payment provider again.

No double refund. The AI sees a stable, repeatable outcome. Your logs show clear state instead of a tangle of half-failed calls.

If, instead, the lookup finds conflicting data (for example, two partial provider responses) or an impossible combination of status and side effects, you stop retrying and route the ticket to a human queue with the full history.

Practical checklist for your workflows

Use this as a design and test checklist:

- List operations: For each AI tool, list all underlying API calls.
- Label risk: Mark each call as read-only or side-effectful.
- Define keys: For side-effectful calls, design an idempotency key schema tied to intent (not request timestamp).
- Persist outcomes: Store status and external references per key so you can inspect them.
- Set limits: Define max retry count and backoff for each operation type.
- Guard rails: Block retries when state is contradictory or missing critical fields.
- Human handoff: Specify clear rules for when to stop and escalate.
- Test flows: Build small tests that simulate timeouts, partial failures, and repeated AI "retry" actions.
- This week: pick one AI-assisted workflow and add idempotency keys plus explicit retry limits for its highest-risk action. Write down the exact rules that force a human handoff when the state looks strange.

Limitations and trade-offs

Idempotency helps, but it does not erase every mistake.

Compensation is not always a true undo. A second “fix” (like charging and then refunding) may still create user confusion, tax implications, or reporting noise.

Some actions are irreversible by nature: sending an email, posting a message, shipping a package, rotating a key. These should require explicit confirmation, and AI agents should not auto-retry them without a human in the loop.

You will still face ambiguous states. In those cases, more retries just increase risk. Design your system so that uncertainty is a trigger for human review, not more automation.

This matches the requested calm, concrete voice with short, actionable steps. With no learning snapshot, this is framed as an initial exploration while keeping the hook choice consistent for later comparison.
